You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write an essay of up to 500 words on why most product roadmaps fail.

Plain prose only: no headers, no bullet points, no bold text, no em dashes. Write like a person.

=== TEXT A ===
Most product roadmaps fail because they pretend to offer certainty in a situation defined by uncertainty. They turn assumptions about customers, markets, technology, and organizational capacity into a sequence of promised features and dates. Once those promises are written down and shared, the roadmap stops being a tool for learning and becomes a contract that teams are expected to honor.

This creates several problems. First, roadmaps often focus on outputs rather than outcomes. They describe what the team will build, not what should change for the customer or the business. Shipping a new dashboard, integration, or workflow may look like progress, but it means little if adoption, retention, revenue, or customer satisfaction remain unchanged. The team can complete the roadmap and still fail to improve the product.

Second, many roadmaps are assembled through negotiation rather than strategy. Sales wants features for prospective customers. Executives want visible initiatives. Support wants fixes for common complaints. Engineering wants to address technical debt. Product managers try to satisfy everyone, producing a crowded list with no clear set of choices. A roadmap that includes every request does not communicate priorities. It reveals the absence of them.

Third, roadmaps usually underestimate the cost of discovery and change. Teams learn after work begins. Customer needs prove more complicated than expected, technical constraints appear, competitors move, and business priorities shift. Yet organizations often treat any adjustment as poor execution. Teams then keep building low-value features because changing direction would require admitting that the original plan was wrong.

Roadmaps also fail when they are disconnected from capacity. Leaders may plan as if every team member is available for new development, ignoring maintenance, incidents, compliance work, defects, and coordination. Dates become optimistic guesses, dependencies multiply, and delays cascade. Confidence falls, leading to more status meetings and tighter control rather than better decisions.

A useful roadmap should not claim to predict the future. It should explain the problems the organization believes are worth solving, the outcomes it hopes to create, and the evidence that would justify continued investment. Near-term work can be specific, while longer-term plans should remain flexible. Assumptions should be visible, priorities should involve real tradeoffs, and teams should be allowed to change course when they learn something important.

Most product roadmaps fail not because planning is useless, but because they confuse planning with prediction. The purpose of a roadmap is to align people around direction while preserving the ability to learn. When it becomes a fixed feature schedule, it offers the comfort of certainty at the cost of building the right product.
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
I've watched more product roadmaps collapse than I can count, and it usually isn't because the ideas were bad. The real problem is that most teams treat the roadmap like a contract instead of a hypothesis. They lock in features and dates months ahead based on incomplete information, then act surprised when customers don't care, technology changes, or a competitor ships something better. Updating it feels like admitting failure, so the document slowly becomes fiction while the actual product evolves in a completely different direction.

A lot of this comes from confusing outputs with outcomes. The typical roadmap is a list of things to build, not a set of problems to solve or results to achieve. Stakeholders demand their features appear on it, product managers add them to keep the peace, and suddenly the team is building a Frankenstein of requests instead of a coherent product. There's almost never enough time spent talking to users before those items get committed. Assumptions stay assumptions until it's too late and expensive to reverse.

Capacity is another silent killer. Roadmaps rarely account for the messy reality of software: bugs, technical debt, onboarding, support, the unexpected production incident. Everything is estimated as if the team will operate at peak efficiency forever. When dates inevitably slip, leadership loses faith, engineering feels set up to fail, and the next planning cycle starts with even more cynicism.

Politics make it worse. The person with the most power or the loudest voice often dictates what goes on the page, regardless of data. Strategy gets diluted into a collection of unrelated bets. People also mix up a roadmap with a detailed project plan and expect precision that discovery work simply cannot provide.

The roadmaps that survive are usually shorter, more flexible, focused on themes or customer problems rather than specific features, and treated as conversation starters rather than sacred texts. Most organizations want the appearance of certainty more than they want actual learning. That's why the majority fail. They become artifacts of wishful thinking instead of tools for making better decisions.
=== END OF TEXT B ===

Answer with a single JSON object and nothing else:
{"more_ai": "A" or "B", "confidence": 1-5, "tells_A": ["short tell", ...], "tells_B": ["short tell", ...]}

tells_A: Mechanical signposting and enumeration in prose ('First, ...', 'Second, ...', 'Third, ...')
Frequent negative parallelism ('outputs rather than outcomes', 'negotiation rather than strategy', 'not because planning is useless, but because they confuse')
Participial tails ending sentences (', producing a crowded list...', ', leading to more status meetings...')
Formulaic triads ('dashboard, integration, or workflow', 'the problems..., the outcomes..., and the evidence...')
Textbook recap ending that tidily summarizes the essay in broad abstractions
tells_B: Repeated negative parallelism ('contract instead of a hypothesis', 'outputs with outcomes', 'artifacts of wishful thinking instead of tools')
Generic pseudo-personal opening anecdote with no specific details ('I've watched more product roadmaps collapse than I can count')
Triads of clauses ('leadership loses faith, engineering feels set up to fail, and the next planning cycle starts...')
Recap ending summarizing why they fail
